title: The Curse of Conceptual Understanding
author: Ashman, Greg
summary: Greg Ashman responds to Bill McCallum's critique of his earlier 'Conceptual understanding is a myth' post, using the exchange to clarify the cognitive science of schema formation and why the term 'conceptual understanding' is both philosophically slippery and pedagogically misleading. The article's central argument is that what educators call 'conceptual understanding' is not a distinct cognitive state separate from procedural knowledge -- it is the same rich schema, built through practice and integration of procedural and declarative knowledge, that allows experts to solve problems automatically. Ashman introduces the 'curse of knowledge' to explain why expert teachers mistakenly believe novices can shortcut schema-building through discovery or meaning-making: experts have forgotten the slow, effortful process that built their own schemas. The piece challenges the Illustrative Mathematics curriculum's foundational premise -- that conceptual and procedural knowledge can be developed simultaneously through discovery -- arguing this misunderstands how schemas work and why working memory constraints make discovery-first approaches inefficient for novices. Ashman ultimately argues that seeking 'understanding' before knowledge is fully automated is epistemically confused: understanding just is the automated, integrated schema, not a separate mental achievement that precedes or accompanies procedural fluency.
points: Schemas stored in long-term memory -- not conscious working memory processes -- are what actually enable expert performance; a student who 'just knows' the answer to an algebra equation has a highly integrated schema, not a flash of insight.

The 'curse of knowledge' explains why experienced teachers misdiagnose novice difficulty: because their own schemas make problems seem trivially obvious, they underestimate how much practice it took to build those schemas and wrongly assume students can take shortcuts.

Ashman argues that 'conceptual understanding' as a distinct pedagogical goal is incoherent because what educators point to as understanding -- the ability to transfer, explain, and apply -- is simply what a well-integrated procedural-declarative schema looks like from the outside.

The Illustrative Mathematics curriculum's claim that students can 'simultaneously build procedural fluency and conceptual understanding' is problematic because it treats two aspects of the same cognitive structure as if they were separate things that can be cultivated independently.

Finding common ground with McCallum is genuinely possible -- both value mathematical reasoning -- but the agreement dissolves when examining whether discovery-first or instruction-first approaches better serve schema formation given working memory constraints.
quotes: Within a fraction of a second of seeing the above equation, they will simply have known that x is equal to six. They will have achieved this not by using working memory resources, but by activating a complex schema for problems like these that is stored in long-term memory.

These schemas are so powerful, they can answer questions before we think to ask them. Yet they represent the slow accumulation of large amounts of integrated knowledge. In this case, for example, an algebra schema must seamlessly integrate with the schema for the six-times-table.

The sheer ease with which individuals who have studied algebra can retrieve this answer leads to a common problem -- the curse of knowledge. We struggle to empathise with those who lack these schemas because it seems so obvious and trivial to us.
That sense of triviality leads to us dismissing the hard work that goes into developing these schemas and can cause us to assume that our students can somehow acquire them without all that work.

Even if you are unconvinced by cognitive load theory, the finding that we can only process about four items at a time in working memory is robust across cognitive science. But what is an item? In the equation above, we can see five symbols. If that surprises you because you read '18' as one item then, again, you should visit an elementary school and see how painstakingly such knowledge is assembled.
Those who suggest it is a waste of time to memorise such maths facts are plainly wrong.
